screens.title: Card taps
screens.text: A university system looks up a student number every time a student taps their card at a venue. New student numbers are issued in increasing order. Which structure would you choose?
screens.reveal: An unsorted list makes every lookup O(n). A plain BST would grow into a chain, because the numbers arrive in increasing order. An AVL tree rebalances after each insertion, so every lookup stays O(log n).

screens.title: Goal
screens.text: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to identify practical applications of AVL trees and justify the choice from their properties.

task.stem: What is the worst-case search cost in a plain BST with n keys?
task.hint: This question checks whether you can justify the choice from the properties of an AVL tree. It guarantees O(log n) search, at the cost of extra work on updates.

options.explanation: A plain BST can become a chain.
O(log n) is the cost in a balanced tree, and a plain BST has no balance guarantee.

screens.title: When an AVL tree is a good fit
points: The data must stay in sorted order, and an in-order traversal lists it in sorted order at any time.
The data is searched often, and a guaranteed O(log n) search matters more than the extra work on updates.
Keys may arrive in sorted or nearly sorted order, which would turn a plain BST into a chain.
Good examples are a word list for a spell checker, an index of student numbers and a contacts list kept in alphabetical order.

screens.title: What it costs
points: Each node uses extra space, because it stores its height or balance factor.
Insertion and deletion take extra time, because they update balance factors and rotate.
This is a time and space trade-off. Balanced trees take longer on updates, but they protect against the worst case.
Red-Black trees are another kind of balanced tree, with a looser balance rule. You may meet them later.

screens.title: Worked example: a contacts list
steps: Is the data searched often? Yes, because names are looked up all day.
Must it stay in order? Yes, because the list is shown alphabetically, and an in-order traversal gives that order.
Can keys arrive sorted? Yes, because contacts are often imported from an alphabetical file, which would make a plain BST a chain.
How often is it updated? Only a few contacts are added each day, so the extra rotation work is small.
An AVL tree fits. It keeps the names sorted and guarantees O(log n) lookups, at a small cost on updates.

task.stem: A spell checker loads 200,000 words once from a dictionary file sorted from A to Z, and then it looks up every word you type. Is an AVL tree a good choice?
task.hint: This question checks whether you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree. An AVL tree suits data that is searched often and must stay in sorted order.

options.text: No. A plain BST is just as fast here, because the words are already sorted.
options.explanation: Sorted input is the worst case for a plain BST. Every word goes right, which gives a chain of 200,000 levels.

options.text: Yes. Lookups are frequent, and the sorted file would turn a plain BST into a chain. An AVL tree keeps lookups O(log n).
options.explanation: The sorted input is exactly the case that the AVL rule protects against.

options.text: Yes, because AVL search uses the balance factors to find words faster.
options.explanation: The choice is right, but the reason is not. A search ignores balance factors, and balance only keeps the tree short.

task.stem: A system appends a record to a log every second, and the whole log is read from start to end once a day. Is an AVL tree a good choice?
task.hint: This question checks whether you can recognise a good fit for an AVL tree. An AVL tree suits data that is searched often and must stay in sorted order.

options.text: Yes. An AVL tree is always the best structure for storing data.
options.explanation: No structure is best for everything. Here the balancing work buys nothing, because nobody searches by key.

options.text: Yes. An AVL tree costs nothing extra compared with a list.
options.explanation: Every insertion updates balance factors and may rotate, and every node stores a height.

options.text: No. Nothing is searched by key, so a simple list that appends at the end does the job without the balancing work.
options.explanation: An AVL tree pays off only when searches by key are frequent.

screens.title: Lesson check
screens.text: This check has one question for each assessment criterion of the lesson's objective. You can re-attempt each question once, and the Hint button is always available.

screens.title: Summary
points: Choose an AVL tree for sorted data that is searched often, especially if keys can arrive in order.
The price is a height in every node and extra work on every update.
If data is rarely searched by key, a simpler structure is better.
